1:
The occasion is agreed, the structure mapped. Adam Clarke dates the psalm during or after the return from Babylon and divides it in four: thanksgiving, prayer, waiting and assurance. John Calvin gives the same shape as an argument: afflicted with new troubles after their return, they first mention their deliverance as a reason why God should not leave the work of his grace unfinished, then complain of the long continuance of their afflictions, and at last triumph in the blessedness promised them. Charles Ellicott grants the opening phrase might only imply a return to former prosperity, but says the context directs us to the exile's end.

Augustine of Hippo reads the psalm through its title. The words for the end direct the heart to Christ, who is the end of the law: fix our gaze on him and we shall not stray, for he is himself the Truth we are eager to reach and the Way by which we run. He then accounts for the tenses: the prophet sings of the future in words of past time, because with God what is future has already happened.

Keil and Delitzsch supply a literary genealogy. The second part of the book of Isaiah was written for the Israel of the exile, and out of it, once the exile had unsealed it, sprang the psalms that recall their common model by their allegorising figurative language and their lofty prophetic thoughts of consolation.

The forgiveness of the second verse is read as ceremony. Clarke renders it thou hast borne, or carried away, the iniquity, an allusion to the scapegoat, and takes the covering to mean that the offensiveness of the sin no longer appears, the whole being put out of sight; on the pause that follows he writes simply that this is true, the return to their own land being the full proof. He carries the metaphor on: the wrath is gathered up and carried away with the iniquities. Ellicott gives the same verb its plainer sense, taken away. John Gill supplies the theology: the iniquity was taken from them and laid on Christ, who bore it so that it shall never return, and the wrath was gathered and poured on the surety.

What the prayer to turn us asks divides five ways. John Wesley wants restoration to their former tranquillity and freedom from the troubles they yet groan under. Ellicott makes it restore us once more, and finds in it the motive of the song: if the captivity had taught its lesson, why did complete freedom from misfortune not follow? Delitzsch denies it means restore us again at all, construing it as turn again to us, a prayer that God manifest himself anew as in former days. Clarke wants the restoration completed, since the people came back in instalments, a few with Zerubbabel and more with Ezra and Nehemiah while great numbers stayed abroad. Gill takes it for converting grace, perhaps for the conversion of the Jews in the latter day.

The questions that follow are treated as arguments, not complaints. C.H. Spurgeon says the psalmist makes bold to plead: we are in time and not eternity, and since time ends, shall the wrath not end with it? Shall sons suffer for their fathers' faults, and punishment become an entailed inheritance? Every word, he says, is an argument, for men in distress never waste words. Gill answers doctrinally: God is angry with the wicked every day and for ever, but his anger with his own people endures only a moment. Matthew Henry notices who is speaking: the church in affliction makes her application to God by direction from God, so ready is he to hear that by his Spirit he indites their petitions and puts words into their mouths. Clarke and Wesley read the reviving nationally, a people becoming numerous again and the rest of the brethren brought home.
8:
The turn from praying to listening is marked by all. Matthew Henry has the psalmist stand on his watch-tower as a prophet did, reading it as a stilling of his own passions: compose thyself, O my soul, in a humble silence; I have spoken enough, now I will hear. If we would have God hear our prayer, he adds, we must be ready to hear his word. C.H. Spurgeon has the poet pause in joyful confidence, since only from God comes the word that speaks peace, men's voices being a plaister far too narrow for the sore.

Peace and folly are glossed narrowly. Charles Ellicott says peace comprehends everything the nation sighed for, that to Christians it has a higher meaning still, which directed this psalm's choice for Christmas Day, and that the folly most probably means idolatry. Adam Clarke reads the folly as abusing God's mercy by sinning any more. John Wesley narrows the saints instead: not all who are called God's people, but only those who are truly such.

That the salvation is near gets a date. John Wesley says he might well call it nigh, since the seventy weeks of the vision were already begun, and that the salvation meant is the redemption by the Messiah, which not only Christian but even Jewish writers find here. Clarke keeps the glory local, then extends it: the worship restored, the temple rebuilt, the divine presence back in place, the second temple, inferior as a building, having the superior glory of being visited by Christ.

The meeting of the four attributes is Clarke's best work here. He would render it more simply, mercy and truth have met on the way, righteousness and peace have embraced, and finds a beauty he thinks unnoticed: mercy and peace on one side, truth and righteousness on the other, truth requiring righteousness and mercy calling for peace. One goes to make inquisition for sin, the other to plead for reconciliation; their differences adjusted and their claims blended, peace and righteousness embrace. Ellicott confirms it from the word itself, used of those who should be friends but whom circumstances have sundered. John Gill has them meet in Christ, in whom grace and truth came.

What springs out of the earth divides them. Keil and Delitzsch make it faithfulness to the covenant, springing up as the fruit of God's faithfulness after that has descended like dew, gracious justice looking down from heaven and dispensing blessing. Ellicott grounds it in the harvest: renewed fertility had re-established a shaken conviction of God's faithfulness, and the righteousness hidden like the sun behind a cloud shows its face again, the verb being used of bending from a window. Clarke reads it of true religion diffused by the preaching of Christ and his apostles. Gill offers three and prefers the last: the gospel, which sprang up at once in Judea as if out of the earth; the truth of grace in the heart; or Christ himself, who though the Lord from heaven may by his incarnation be said to spring out of the earth.

The closing promises are read materially and morally at once. Clarke takes the good thing for the supreme good man has vainly searched for through all his generations, the land yielding its increase in the conversion of the nations. Ellicott would render the last verse righteousness shall walk in front of him and follow in his steps, and observes that nothing is more instructive than the blending of material and moral blessings here, which do go together, as national experience testifies; he closes with an English ode to Duty, before whom flowers laugh on their beds. Gill takes the righteousness for a righteous person, following a rabbi, and suggests John the Baptist. Wesley agrees it goes as a harbinger, fulfilling all righteousness and causing us to walk in the ways wherein he walks.
